narrative:
The model estimates a 30% chance that you will not pass your final year. Although that is below a coin flip, the school treats it as enough risk to require remedial courses now, because they are meant to reduce the chance of failure before it becomes final. The strongest signal in your profile is that you have no past class failures; this works in your favor and is the most influential factor in the assessment. The second most influential factor is your intention to continue to higher education, which also points toward passing and matches every student who passed in the comparison group. The third is your low amount of free time after school, which again leans toward passing rather than failing.

What pushes the overall picture toward risk is not those top three factors but the wider combination of circumstances: you study fewer than two hours a week, while most students who passed studied two to five hours; you receive no family educational support, although 62% of passers did; and your parents’ education is primary level, which is less common among passers. Your zero absences and no past failures are positives.

To improve, use the remedial support to build a regular weekly study routine above two hours, ask your family or school for structured help, and keep your higher-education goal visible. Continue attending every class and use your limited free time deliberately rather than adding more commitments.
